summary: For ages 10–11: build the idea that light TRAVELS along a continuous straight path through the dark space between a source and an object — not merely that light 'is' wherever it is bright. Learners test rectilinear travel by trying to violate it (holes must align, light won't turn corners), then USE straight-line travel to explain why a shadow reproduces the object's outline. The target is deploying the straight-line model to predict and explain, not reciting the slogan. The ray is taught explicitly as a model of the path and its direction, not a physical sliver of light.
misconceptions: Light isn't thought of as travelling at all — it simply 'is' wherever it is bright.
Light exists only in the bright regions, not in the space in between as it journeys.
Light bends or curves around edges/corners (so why would shadows be sharp?).
A 'light ray' is a real, physical thin sliver of light rather than a model of the path's direction.
Light is 'made of rays added together'.
Light only travels in straight lines when it comes from a mirror or a laser, not in general.

activities.title: Fire a beam, block it, and discover light won't turn corners
steps: Aim a torch across a darkened scene so the beam's straight-edged path becomes visible (use a slightly hazy/dusty or smoky room, where particles scatter some light to your eyes, or draw the beam with straight ray lines, so the travelling path shows).

Place a card with a single hole in the beam's path. Slide the hole until light passes through and reaches a small 'eye' on the far side; note it only gets through when the hole sits on the straight line between torch and eye.
Nudge the hole off that line and observe the light is blocked — it will not bend to find the gap.

Drop an opaque shape into the beam and observe the light passing straight past its edges, throwing a shadow on a screen whose outline matches the shape as seen from the torch (it may be bigger or stretched depending on distances and how the shape and screen are angled).
Try to 'make the shadow wrap round the back of the object' or 'bend the light round the corner' — and find you cannot.
activities.insight: Light travels in straight lines through the space between source and object; a shadow has the object's outline (as seen from the source) because light travels straight past the edges and does not turn corners into the space behind the object, unless something such as a mirror redirects it.

activities.title: Three holes in a line — predict, then break the alignment
steps: Line up three cards, each with a small hole punched in the middle, and shine a torch so light passes through all three holes to your eye (threading string through the holes helps show the straight line).
Before moving anything, predict: if you slide the MIDDLE card sideways, will you still see the light? Say why first.
Slide the middle card off-line and check your prediction.
Explain what the result proves about how light travels.
Discuss: when you see the beam in dusty air, are you seeing the light itself or the dust it lights up?
activities.insight: Light reaches the eye only when the holes are lined up; the offset-hole result contradicts a 'light bends to find its way' model and supports the model that light travels in straight lines.

activities.title: Draw and use ray diagrams to predict a shadow
steps: Draw rays with a ruler as straight lines starting from the light source, putting a direction arrow on every ray.
Draw rays grazing the edges of an opaque object and continuing to a screen to show where the shadow falls and why its outline matches the object.
Predict the shadow's outline for a given shape BEFORE revealing or checking the actual result, then compare.
Explain in words why the shadow reproduces the object's outline, referring to the straight rays past its edges.
activities.insight: A correct source–object–screen ray diagram with ruler-straight, arrowed rays from the source both represents straight-line travel and lets you predict shadow shape.

activities.title: You can't see round corners
steps: Hold a rolled tube to your eye and confirm you can only see what is straight ahead through it.
Try to use the tube to see something off to one side, around a corner — and find you cannot.
Explain how this shows that light travels in straight lines from an object to your eye.
activities.insight: Because light travels in straight lines from an object to your eye, you cannot see round a corner without something like a mirror to redirect the light.

checkQuestion: You line up three cards, each with a small hole punched in the middle, and shine a torch so you can see the light through all three holes. Now you slide the MIDDLE card sideways a little. Will you still see the light coming through? Explain what this tells you about how light travels.
checkAnswer: No — you no longer see the light. Light travels in straight lines, so it can only pass through all three holes when they are lined up straight; it cannot bend to get through the offset middle hole.
